enriched_description: A freshwater cyprinid fish with an elongated, laterally compressed body covered in small, deeply embedded cycloid scales that give a smooth, slimy texture. Coloration ranges from olive-green to golden-bronze on the dorsal surface, fading to pale yellow-white ventrally. The head is small relative to body length with a blunt, slightly downturned mouth equipped with two short barbels at each corner. Eyes are small, positioned laterally, with a reddish-orange iris. Dorsal fin is short and rounded with 3-4 unbranched and 8-9 branched rays; caudal fin is truncate to slightly emarginate. Body proportions: depth approximately 3-4 times standard length. The lateral line is complete and distinctly visible as a pale curved line running mid-laterally from operculum to caudal peduncle. Fins exhibit a dark gray to olive hue without prominent markings. Skin texture is characteristically mucous-coated, distinguishing it from rough-scaled cyprinids.

A small cyprinid fish with a laterally compressed, ovoid to fusiform body covered in large, easily visible cycloid scales. Domestic and feral specimens display vivid coloration ranging from metallic orange-red to golden-yellow, with some individuals exhibiting calico patterns of orange, white, and black patches. Wild-type specimens are dull olive-green dorsally with silvery-white ventral surfaces. The head is short with a terminal mouth lacking barbels (distinguishing from tench). Eyes are large and prominent, positioned high on the head. Dorsal fin is long-based with 15-20 rays, extending from mid-back; caudal fin is deeply forked in wild types but may be double-tailed or fantail in ornamental varieties. Body depth is approximately 2-3 times standard length. Scales exhibit a reflective, metallic sheen under illumination. Fin membranes are translucent with coloration matching the body. The opercular region may display an iridescent golden patch. Proportions vary significantly between wild and domesticated morphs, with ornamental breeds showing exaggerated body depth and fin elongation.

class_name: great white shark, white shark, man-eater, man-eating shark, Carcharodon carcharias
enriched_description: A large mackerel shark with a robust, torpedo-shaped (fusiform) body covered in dermal denticles that create a rough, sandpaper-like texture. Exhibits countershading coloration: dark gray to slate-gray dorsally, sharply demarcated from a clean white ventral surface along the lateral midline. The snout is conical and pointed. Eyes are large, round, and black without a nictitating membrane. Mouth is wide and arched, containing 5 rows of large, triangular, serrated teeth (up to 7 cm in length) arranged in a continuous cutting edge. Five prominent gill slits are visible anterior to the pectoral fins. Pectoral fins are large, falcate (sickle-shaped), and positioned low on the body. The first dorsal fin is tall and triangular, originating posterior to the pectoral fin free tip; the second dorsal fin is markedly smaller. Caudal fin is lunate (crescent-shaped) with nearly symmetrical upper and lower lobes, adapted for sustained high-speed swimming. Body proportions: total length can exceed 6 meters, with head comprising approximately one-fifth of total length. The lateral line system is visible as a series of pore openings along the flanks. No prominent body markings or spots; the uniform gray-white contrast is a key diagnostic feature.

A large requiem shark with a broad, blunt snout and a stocky, cylindrical body covered in rough dermal denticles. Coloration is distinctive: grayish-blue to greenish-gray dorsally with a pale gray to white ventral surface. The most diagnostic feature is the presence of dark gray to black transverse bars, spots, and stripes along the flanks and dorsal surface, resembling tiger striping; these markings are most prominent in juveniles and fade with age but remain visible in adults. The mouth is wide with heavily serrated, curved teeth exhibiting a distinctive hooked tip. Five gill slits are present. Pectoral fins are broad and rounded. The first dorsal fin is relatively small and positioned far posterior, originating over or behind the pectoral fin insertion. A prominent interdorsal ridge runs along the midline between the two dorsal fins. Caudal fin is asymmetrical with a well-developed lower lobe and a pronounced subterminal notch on the upper lobe. Body proportions: adults typically 3-5 meters, with a broad head width approximately one-third of body depth. The combination of transverse body markings and blunt snout distinguishes this species from other large sharks.

A medium-sized shark with the most distinctive morphological feature among elasmobranchs: a laterally expanded, dorsoventrally flattened cephalofoil (head extension) resembling a hammer or T-shape. The cephalofoil width ranges from 25-30% of total body length. Eyes are positioned at the extreme lateral tips of the cephalofoil, providing nearly 360-degree vertical vision. Nostrils are located at the anterior margin of the cephalofoil, separated by a broad medial indentation. Body is streamlined and fusiform, covered in fine dermal denticles giving a rough texture. Coloration is olive-gray to brown dorsally, fading to white ventrally, with no prominent markings or stripes. The first dorsal fin is tall and falcate, originating over or slightly anterior to the pectoral fin insertion. Pectoral fins are moderately falcate. Caudal fin is asymmetrical with a prominent upper lobe and subterminal notch. Five gill slits are visible on the ventrolateral surface. Body proportions: total length typically 2.5-4 meters depending on species within the Sphyrnidae family. The unique cephalofoil structure, combined with the absence of body markings and the tall first dorsal fin, provides unambiguous visual identification.

A sluggish, bottom-dwelling elasmobranch with a distinctive flattened, disc-like body formed by the fusion of enlarged pectoral fins to the head and trunk. The body disc is nearly circular to oval, with a smooth, soft, gelatinous texture lacking the rough dermal denticles typical of sharks. Coloration is uniform dark brown, gray, or reddish-brown dorsally, often with mottled or marbled patterns providing camouflage against sandy or muddy substrates; ventral surface is pale white to cream. The tail is thick, muscular, and shorter than the body disc, terminating in a well-developed caudal fin. Two dorsal fins are present on the tail (distinguishing from stingrays which lack dorsal fins). Eyes are small and positioned dorsally on the head; spiracles are large and prominent, located immediately posterior to the eyes, adapted for benthic respiration. The most diagnostic internal feature (externally invisible but taxonomically critical) is the pair of large electric organs derived from branchial muscle, occupying the pectoral region on each side of the head, capable of discharging 8-220 volts. Mouth and nostrils are ventrally positioned. Body proportions: disc width typically 30-60 cm, with tail length approximately equal to disc length. The combination of circular disc shape, thick tail with two dorsal fins, and absence of a venomous spine distinguishes electric rays from stingrays.

A large, venomous elasmobranch ray with a dorsoventrally flattened body disc formed by broad, wing-like pectoral fins fused to the head. The disc shape varies from diamond to circular depending on species, with a smooth to granular dorsal surface covered in small dermal denticles or tubercles. Coloration is typically olive-brown, gray, or sandy dorsally, often with a uniform appearance or subtle mottling; ventral surface is white to pale cream. The most diagnostic feature is one or more serrated, venomous caudal spines (barbs) located on the dorsal surface of the tail near its base, capable of inflicting severe wounds. The tail is elongated, whip-like, and significantly longer than the body disc (often 2-3 times disc length), lacking dorsal fins (distinguishing from electric rays). Eyes and spiracles are positioned dorsally on the head. Mouth, nostrils, and five gill slits are ventrally positioned. The disc surface may exhibit small thorn-like denticles along the midline in some species. Body proportions: disc width ranges from 15 cm to over 2 meters depending on species. The combination of whip-like tail, venomous caudal spine(s), absence of dorsal fins, and ventral gill slits provides definitive identification.

An adult male bird (Gallus gallus domesticus) characterized by prominent secondary sexual dimorphic features. The head bears a large, fleshy, serrated comb (single or rose type) that is bright red to crimson, standing erect and extending from the base of the beak to the posterior crown. A pair of pendulous red wattles hangs from the lower mandible. The beak is short, curved, and horn-colored (yellow to gray). Eyes are round with a reddish-brown iris and a distinct pale orbital ring. Plumage is highly variable by breed but typically exhibits iridescent green-black feathers on the neck (hackles) and saddle, with contrasting body feathers in red, brown, black, or white. The tail features long, arching, iridescent sickle feathers (greater and lesser coverts) that curve upward and backward, a key male diagnostic trait. Legs are unfeathered, scaly, with a rough keratinous texture, colored yellow to gray, bearing three forward-facing toes and one rear-facing hallux, each with a sharp curved claw. A prominent spur (calcaneal process) projects from the posterior tarsometatarsus, increasing in size with age. Body proportions: males are larger than females, with a more upright posture, broader shoulders, and longer hackle and saddle feathers. The comb size, spur presence, and sickle tail feathers are the primary visual markers distinguishing males from hens.

An adult female bird (Gallus gallus domesticus) exhibiting secondary sexual characteristics distinct from the male. The head bears a small, fleshy comb that is pale red to pinkish, often floppy or partially developed, significantly smaller than the male's erect comb. Wattles are reduced or absent. The beak is short, slightly curved, and horn-colored (yellow to gray). Eyes are round with a reddish-brown iris and a pale orbital ring. Plumage is generally more uniform and subdued than the male, lacking iridescent hackle and saddle feathers; body feathers are typically brown, red, black, white, or barred depending on breed, with a rounded, compact contour optimized for egg-laying and brooding. The tail is short with straight, non-arched feathers, lacking the male's characteristic sickle feathers. Legs are unfeathered, scaly with a rough keratinous texture, colored yellow to gray, bearing three forward-facing toes and one rear-facing hallux with curved claws. Spurs are absent or present only as small, undeveloped bumps on the tarsometatarsus. Body proportions: females are smaller and more compact than males, with a broader, deeper abdomen (vent region) adapted for egg production. The small comb, absence of sickle tail feathers, lack of spurs, and broader abdominal profile are the primary visual markers distinguishing hens from cocks.

A large, flightless ratite bird with the most massive body and longest legs of any living bird. Adults stand 2.1-2.8 meters tall and weigh 63-145 kg. The body is covered in soft, fluffy, filamentous plumage lacking the interlocking barbules of flying birds, giving a shaggy, disheveled appearance. Males exhibit black body plumage with white primary and secondary wing feathers and white tail plumes; females are uniformly grayish-brown. The neck is elongated (approximately 1 meter), nearly featherless, with pink to gray skin that may flush red during courtship. The head is small relative to body size, with large eyes (approximately 5 cm diameter, the largest of any terrestrial vertebrate) framed by long, prominent eyelashes. The beak is broad, flat, and horn-colored. Wings are reduced, with two functional digits bearing claws, used for balance and display. The most distinctive feature is the pair of extremely long, powerful legs covered in scaly skin, each with only two toes (didactyl condition unique among birds): a large inner toe bearing a 10 cm hoof-like claw and a smaller outer toe. Legs are pinkish in males, grayish in females. The tail is a short tuft of decorative plumes. Body proportions: leg length exceeds body length; neck comprises approximately one-third of total height. The combination of enormous size, two-toed feet, elongated featherless neck, and shaggy plumage provides unambiguous identification among all bird species.
